domains.name: IT Roles Library
domains.summary: A working map of IT roles across support, engineering, security, and data: what each role owns, how career ladders differentiate levels, and how skills matrices expose coverage gaps. Descriptive of common industry structures, not a prescription; the course confers no certificate.

scenarios.title: Where Does This Ticket Go?
scenarios.situation: A user cannot print to the office printer. Tier-1 asks whether the ticket belongs to the help desk, desktop support, or the systems administrator — and the printer queue lives on a print server.
scenarios.prompt: How should the ticket be routed?
evidence: L1 (help desk): first contact, triage, remote fixes, password resets, known-issue resolution. L2 (desktop support): hands-on hardware/OS issues at the desk. Sysadmin: servers, infrastructure, and services many users share.
One user cannot print; the print server itself is healthy and others print fine.
choices: Help desk owns initial triage and remote fixes (driver, queue, permissions); escalate to desktop support only if it needs hands-on work at the machine — the sysadmin is not needed while the shared print service is healthy.
Send every ticket straight to the sysadmin; they are the most senior and will fix it fastest.
The help desk only resets passwords, so skip them and page desktop support immediately.
Desktop support owns all printing because printers are hardware.
scenarios.why: Tiered support exists to match cost to complexity: L1 resolves the common cases with remote tooling, L2 handles what needs hands, and sysadmins protect shared infrastructure from one-off tickets. Routing everything upward burns expensive specialist time and teaches users to bypass triage.
scenarios.hint: Match the scope of the failure — one user versus a shared service — to the scope each tier owns.

scenarios.title: Staffing the Customer Portal
scenarios.situation: A startup needs a customer portal: a web UI, an API, and a database. The founder wants to hire a single full-stack developer to do everything, including the security review, to save money.
scenarios.prompt: What is the sound staffing call?
evidence: Front-end: UI/UX implementation. Back-end: APIs, business logic, data. Full-stack: working breadth across both — depth in each varies by individual.
One person designing, building, and security-reviewing their own work removes every independent check on the highest-risk parts.
choices: A full-stack developer can prototype the portal, but plan for front-end/back-end specialization plus an independent security review as scope grows — full-stack means breadth, not infinite depth or self-review.
One full-stack developer covers everything indefinitely; specialization is just big-company overhead.
Front-end developers cannot touch APIs by definition, so hire two people minimum on day one.
Hire only back-end; the UI is trivial and security review is optional for MVPs.
scenarios.why: Full-stack describes range, not unlimited capacity: as a product grows, the depth required in each layer (and in security) exceeds what one generalist sustains. The pragmatic path is a generalist to start, specialists as complexity demands, and always a second pair of eyes on security.
scenarios.hint: Ask which parts of this project get worse — not better — when the same person does all of them.

scenarios.title: Who Builds the Pipeline?
scenarios.situation: An executive asks the new data scientist to 'build the nightly ETL' feeding the dashboards. Three weeks later the scientist is debugging Airflow workers instead of modeling churn.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong in the role assignment?
evidence: Data engineer: pipelines, ETL/ELT, warehouse modeling, data platform reliability. Data analyst: BI, dashboards, decision support on curated data. Data scientist: statistical models and experiments on prepared data.
A specialist salary spent on infrastructure plumbing is the most expensive way to build a pipeline — and the modeling work the hire was made for is stalled.
choices: Pipeline construction is data engineering work: reassign the ETL to a data engineer (or hire/contract one) and return the scientist to modeling on curated data.
Data scientists do it all — infrastructure struggle is just part of the job.
Analysts should write production ETL since they know the dashboards best.
Hire a DBA; pipelines are just databases with extra steps.
scenarios.why: Each data role optimizes for a different output: reliable data movement, trusted insights, or predictive models. Misassigning pipeline engineering to a scientist wastes specialist leverage in both directions — bad pipelines and no models. Clear role boundaries let each craft compound.
scenarios.hint: Match the deliverable — a reliable nightly data feed — to the role whose core output that is.

scenarios.title: Who Owns the 3 A.M. Page?
scenarios.situation: After a major outage, the DevOps team and the SRE team each insist the other owns production reliability. Deploys are fast, incidents are frequent, and nobody can say what 'reliable enough' means.
evidence: SRE: applies software engineering to reliability — SLOs, error budgets, incident response. DevOps: a culture and practice of collaboration plus automation across dev and ops. Platform team: builds the internal delivery platform others use.
Velocity without a reliability target means every deploy is a gamble; finger-pointing fills the vacuum where an SLO should be.
choices: Define it explicitly: SRE owns reliability targets (SLOs/error budgets) and the production incident response; DevOps/platform provides the delivery platform both build on — overlapping tooling, distinct accountability, and an error budget that gates velocity.
Merge the titles — DevOps and SRE are identical, so the distinction is the problem.
Declare that developers should never be paged, which resolves the dispute.
Whoever deployed last owns everything, no further definition needed.
scenarios.why: Reliability arguments are really arguments about unspoken targets. SRE makes the target explicit (SLOs) and spends the error budget deliberately; DevOps describes how teams collaborate to ship. Naming who sets the target, who responds, and what throttles velocity ends the turf war.
scenarios.hint: The teams are not arguing about tools — what measurable thing has nobody defined?

scenarios.title: Staffing the SOC
scenarios.situation: A company is building a 24/7 security operations center. The plan staffs only L1 alert triage analysts plus a GRC manager — no L2 investigators, no L3 hunters, no detection engineer.
scenarios.prompt: What is the critical gap in this plan?
evidence: L1: triage alerts, follow playbooks, escalate. L2: investigate, scope, and contain incidents. L3: threat hunting, forensics, and building new detections.
GRC (governance, risk, compliance) manages risk frameworks, audits, and policy — it does not investigate intrusions.
choices: Add L2 investigation and L3/detection-engineering capability: L1 triages, L2 investigates and contains, L3 hunts and builds detections — and keep GRC on governance, not incident response.
L1 analysts can handle advanced intrusions if given enough dashboards.
The GRC manager can double as technical incident commander during a breach.
Buying a SIEM removes the need for L2/L3 staffing.
scenarios.why: A SOC without investigation depth is an alert-forwarding service: L1 escalates into a void, dwell time grows, and the GRC manager — skilled at risk frameworks, not forensics — becomes a bottleneck. Tools amplify analysts; they do not replace the tier that asks 'what actually happened here?'
scenarios.hint: Trace a real intrusion from alert to containment: which of those steps can the current staffing actually perform?

scenarios.title: Senior or Staff?
scenarios.situation: A promotion case: an engineer ships features quickly and mentors interns, but all work stays within one team and designs never face cross-team review. The manager proposes staff engineer.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct leveling call?
evidence: Senior: strong execution and mentoring, scope of a team. Staff: technical leadership across teams — owning ambiguous problems, setting direction, multiplying others. Principal: org-wide impact.
Fast delivery plus intern mentoring demonstrates senior-level execution; nothing in the packet shows multi-team scope or ambiguous-problem ownership.
choices: Level at senior: the scope demonstrated is team-level execution and mentoring. Define the staff path explicitly — multi-team technical leadership on ambiguous problems — so the engineer knows what to grow into.
Promote to staff; tenure and velocity decide level.
Staff just means a senior who codes faster, so the packet qualifies.
Levels are meaningless; title everyone 'engineer' and move on.
scenarios.why: IC levels differentiate on scope, ambiguity, and influence — not speed or years. Inflating the level for strong team-scope work compresses the ladder: future staff candidates have no bar to clear, and the engineer gets expectations they were never shown. A clear, written bar protects both.
scenarios.hint: Ask whose work changes if this engineer disappeared: one team, or several?

scenarios.title: The Matrix Has a Single Point of Failure
scenarios.situation: Your platform team's skills matrix shows exactly one person can perform Terraform state surgery and only one holds the CI signing keys. That person starts a two-week vacation the day a state corruption incident hits.
scenarios.prompt: What should the matrix have driven you to do before this happened?
evidence: A skills matrix maps who holds each critical capability at what depth — its purpose is making coverage gaps and bus-factor risks visible, not ranking people.
State surgery is blocked, signing keys are unreachable, and the team is reverse-engineering both under incident pressure.
choices: Treat single-coverage critical skills as risks to retire: pair on the next real task, write runbooks, rotate the duty, and re-measure — the matrix exists to drive deliberate cross-training, not to decorate a wiki.
Forbid vacations during on-call rotations.
Delete the matrix; it only creates anxiety about irreplaceable people.
Hire a second expert and change nothing about how knowledge is shared.
scenarios.why: Bus factor is a process failure, not a personnel one. Headcount without knowledge transfer just creates two silos; the fix is making the tacit explicit (runbooks), exercised (rotation), and verified (re-measured matrix). The matrix did its job by showing the risk — the failure was not acting on it.
scenarios.hint: The matrix already told you this would happen. What action does that warning require?

scenarios.title: Splitting the IT Generalist
scenarios.situation: At 60 people, one 'IT manager' does help desk, networking, security, and vendor management. Growth to 150 is planned, patches are slipping, and the generalist is burning out.
scenarios.prompt: How should the role structure evolve?
evidence: Generalists win early (breadth, speed); past roughly 75-100 people, blended roles create conflicts — the same person cannot credibly audit the systems they administer, and everything becomes their job.
Missed patches signal security has no dedicated owner; burnout signals the load exceeds one human; growth will multiply both.
choices: Split into role families with clear ownership — e.g., support lead, infrastructure/sysadmin, security — phased with hiring and a written RACI so nothing falls between roles during the transition.
Hire three more generalists with the same blended job description.
Outsource everything to an MSP immediately with no internal ownership.
Promote the generalist to CIO and keep the duties exactly as they are.
scenarios.why: Specialization is how organizations buy focus: security needs an owner whose job is not also the help desk queue, and infrastructure needs someone not context-switching every ticket. A phased split with explicit handoffs avoids the classic failure — reorganizing on paper while the same person still does everything.
scenarios.hint: Ask which two of the current duties are in active conflict when performed by the same person.

lessons.title: IT Roles Library — Core concepts
concepts: Support is tiered by scope: L1 help desk triages and resolves common issues remotely, L2 desktop support handles hands-on hardware/OS problems, and sysadmins own shared infrastructure — escalate with context, not just the ticket.

Engineering roles describe focus, not rank: front-end owns the interface, back-end owns APIs and data, full-stack spans both with varying depth. SRE owns reliability via SLOs and error budgets; platform teams build the internal paved road.

Data roles split by output: data engineers build reliable pipelines and warehouses, analysts turn curated data into decisions, scientists build models and experiments. Misassigning pipeline work to a scientist wastes specialist leverage twice.

Security roles split by function: SOC analysts detect and respond in tiers (triage, investigate, hunt), security engineers build and harden controls, and GRC governs risk, audit, and policy — governance is not incident response.

IC career ladders (associate to senior to staff to principal) differentiate on scope, ambiguity, and influence — not tenure or speed. Management is a separate track, not a promotion from the best individual contributor.

A skills matrix maps who holds each critical capability and at what depth; its value is exposing single points of failure so you can retire them with pairing, runbooks, and rotation — never as a ranking tool.

example.code:
skill: terraform-state-surgery
criticality: high
coverage:
  - person: a.rivera
    depth: 3  # can teach it
  - person: j.chen
    depth: 1  # shadowing
bus_factor: 1
remediation: pair j.chen on next real incident; write runbook; re-measure in 30d
example.walkthrough: One line per critical skill, honest depth ratings, and an explicit bus factor turn tribal knowledge into a visible risk register. The remediation field is the point: the matrix exists to drive cross-training actions with dates, not to decorate a wiki.

pitfalls: Common trap: title inflation — calling every hire 'senior' compresses the ladder and leaves no bar for genuine staff-level scope.
Common trap: using 'full-stack' as an excuse to skip specialists and independent security review as the product grows.
Common trap: promoting the best engineer into management by default — leadership of people is a different craft from technical depth.
Common trap: building the skills matrix once and never re-measuring — coverage rots as people leave and systems change.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

labs.title: Write a Leveled Role Definition
labs.objective: Draft a complete, leveled role definition for a back-end engineer (associate through senior) that a hiring manager could actually post.
steps: Write the mission: one paragraph on what this role owns in the organization.
List 5-7 concrete responsibilities (APIs, data modeling, testing, on-call, security basics).
Add must-have skills and nice-to-have skills, naming real technologies generically (e.g., 'a relational database', not a vendor pitch).
Define level expectations for associate, mid, and senior: scope, autonomy, and mentoring — in observable behaviors, not years.
Run a self-review: grep the file for each required heading and confirm nothing is a single vague bullet.

checks.hint: grep -i for headings like responsibilities, skills, and level expectations to verify structure.

labs.title: Build a Skills Matrix and Find the Gaps
labs.objective: Build a team skills matrix as a CSV, compute coverage per skill, and produce a remediation plan for every single point of failure.
steps: Create matrix.csv with columns person,skill,depth (depth 1=shadowing, 2=independent, 3=can teach) for a fictional 5-person platform team across 8 critical skills.
Use awk to count, per skill, how many people have depth >= 2.
List every skill with coverage below 2 — these are your single points of failure.
For each gap, write one remediation line: pairing assignment, runbook to write, or rotation to schedule, with a re-measure date.
Save the plan as matrix-remediation.md and verify the gap list matches the awk output.

checks.hint: Have awk print each skill with its count of depth>=2 holders so gaps are visible.

simulations.title: Who Owns This Outage?
simulations.brief: The VPN is down for 200 users. Three teams are pointing at each other. Diagnose the ownership failure.

steps.symptom: VPN down 90 minutes. Network team: 'The servers are fine.' Systems team: 'The network is fine.' Help desk: 200 tickets and no updates.
evidence: VPN service has no named owner — it predates the chart
Nobody was alerted; users reported it
A firewall rule push Friday night — change ticket has no service owner listed
options: The firewall change caused it — roll it back and move on
The ownership gap caused the 90 minutes: no service owner means no monitoring, no change accountability, and no communication — the outage is a roles failure wearing a technical mask
Hire more help desk staff to handle the ticket volume
steps.explain: The technical trigger (firewall rule) is secondary. Ninety minutes of silence comes from the missing role: no service owner, no monitoring ownership, no comms owner. Fix the RACI and the next outage gets a 5-minute response.

steps.symptom: VPN restored. The post-mortem needs exactly one roles change that prevents recurrence. Which?
evidence: Name a service owner / buy a new VPN / add headcount
options: Name a service owner for the VPN with explicit accountability: monitoring, change approval, and user communication
steps.explain: A named service owner with the three accountabilities (monitor, approve changes, communicate) converts every future incident from chaos to procedure. Tools don't own services; people do.

steps.symptom: The CIO asks how to find the OTHER unowned services before they fail. What's the method?
evidence: Every production service gets an owner without boiling the ocean
options: Audit all 400 services immediately in one big project
Require an owner field on every change ticket and incident: unowned services reveal themselves at the exact moments they matter, then backfill systematically
Assume the critical ones are already owned
steps.explain: Let incidents and changes surface the gaps: mandatory owner fields turn every ticket into a coverage audit. Backfill the revealed gaps quarterly. Coverage emerges from process, not from a heroic one-time audit.

simulations.debrief: Most 'technical' outages are roles failures: unowned services, unassigned monitoring, unnamed communicators. The roles library exists so the next outage meets an owner, not a pointing contest.

simulations.title: The Career Fork
simulations.brief: You're a tier-2 support engineer with three years in. Two paths open: deep specialist or people-leading manager. Choose with a skills matrix, not vibes.

steps.text: Your skills matrix: troubleshooting 9/10, scripting 7/10, mentoring juniors 8/10, architecture 4/10, stakeholder politics 3/10. The specialist track (SRE) needs architecture 8+; the manager track needs stakeholder skills 7+. Your move?

choices.label: Push for the SRE role now — specialists earn more
choices.feedback: You'd enter senior interviews with architecture at 4/10. The rejections will be polite and unanimous.

choices.label: Map the gaps honestly: 6 months building architecture depth (homelab, certs, project work), then apply
choices.feedback: The matrix becomes a plan: architecture 4→7 via deliberate projects, scripting 7→8 via automation wins. You apply when the matrix says so.

choices.label: Take the team-lead opening — management is the only real promotion
choices.feedback: With stakeholder skills at 3/10, you'd be a lead who can't shield the team or negotiate scope. The team suffers and so do you.

steps.text: Two SRE interviews, two rejections: 'strong troubleshooting, not enough systems design.' What's the repair?

choices.label: Blame the interviewers — leetcode-style system design is broken
choices.feedback: Maybe, but the market doesn't care about your critique. The gap is real regardless of the interview format.

choices.label: Treat the rejections as a free skills audit: build the missing architecture depth in public (blog, homelab, open source) and re-apply in 6 months
choices.feedback: Rejections are data. Six months of visible building converts 'not enough' into a portfolio.

steps.text: Three months as team lead: you're drowning in stakeholder meetings, the team's velocity dropped, and your best engineer just quit citing 'no technical direction'. Diagnose.

choices.label: Work longer hours — leads are supposed to absorb pain
choices.feedback: Hours don't fix a skills gap. The team needs technical direction and stakeholder shielding you can't yet provide.

choices.label: Step back to senior IC, keep mentoring (your 8/10), and deliberately train stakeholder skills before trying leadership again
choices.feedback: The mature move: retreat to strength, train the weakness deliberately. Leadership will still be there when the matrix is ready.

steps.text: Six months later: architecture 7/10, two automation projects in production, a blog with real readers. The SRE loop invites you back. Final interview question: 'Why should we hire a support engineer as an SRE?'

choices.label: 'Because I learn fast and work hard.'
choices.feedback: Everyone says this. You have something better — say it.

choices.label: 'Because I've spent three years debugging production from the user side — I know how systems fail in ways dashboards miss. Here's the matrix, the projects, and the post-mortems to prove it.'
choices.feedback: You turned the 'support' background into the differentiator: failure-mode intuition that pure-infra hires lack. Hired.

simulations.debrief: Career moves are skills-matrix operations: measure honestly, train the specific gaps, apply when the matrix — not your impatience — says ready. And your history is an asset when you frame it as one.

simulations.title: Escalate the Incident
simulations.brief: Order the incident escalation ladder from first responder to executive — who gets involved when.

steps.context: A P2 incident is degrading checkout. Order the escalation path.
items: Tier 1 support: acknowledge, run the runbook, contain what you can
Tier 2 / on-call engineer: deeper diagnosis, first code-level fixes
Service owner: authorize risky mitigations, own customer communication
Incident commander: coordinate multiple teams, manage the war room
Executive sponsor: engaged only if customer impact crosses the business threshold

simulations.debrief: Escalation is about matching authority to impact: runbooks first, engineers second, owners for risky calls, commanders for coordination, executives for business thresholds. Skipping levels wastes everyone's time.

simulations.title: Audit the Access Review
simulations.brief: The quarterly access review has 3 violations hiding in plain sight. Find them.

steps.config:
# access-review.conf — Q3
ceo_admin = true                # line 2
intern_prod_db = write          # line 3
mfa_required = all_users        # line 4
termd_employee = active         # line 5
break_glass = logged            # line 6
vendor_support = standing_admin # line 7
reviews = quarterly             # line 8

issues.description: Intern has WRITE on the production database — violates least privilege catastrophically.
issues.fix: intern_prod_db = none; interns get anonymized staging data.

issues.description: Terminated employee still active — the offboarding process failed and nobody noticed for a quarter.
issues.fix: termd_employee = disabled immediately; tie deprovisioning to HR termination events.

issues.description: Vendor holds standing admin — persistent third-party privileged access with no expiry.
issues.fix: vendor_support = just-in-time elevation with ticket linkage and auto-expiry.

simulations.debrief: Lines 2, 4, 6, 8 are defensible (CEO admin with MFA, logged break-glass, quarterly reviews). The violations: intern write on prod, a ghost account, and standing vendor admin. Access reviews exist to catch exactly these.

simulations.title: The Hiring Panel
simulations.brief: You're hiring a junior SOC analyst. Two finalists, one headcount. The panel is split. Break the tie correctly.

steps.text: Finalist A: CS degree, 3.9 GPA, polished, aced the trivia questions, no homelab. Finalist B: no degree, works help desk, maintains a detection-rules GitHub with 200 stars, fumbled one trivia question but debugged a live log sample brilliantly. The panel is split 2-2. Your vote?

choices.label: A — the degree and polish predict reliability
choices.feedback: You've hired a credential. In six months A knows the playbook; B would have WRITTEN a better one.

choices.label: B — demonstrated skill (detection rules, live debugging) beats credentials for this role
choices.feedback: The GitHub is a work sample; the live debug was a job trial. B has already done the job in public.

choices.label: Abstain — let the panel majority decide
choices.feedback: Abstention is a decision to let noise decide. The hiring manager's job is judgment.

steps.text: A is hired. Month four: A escalates everything, writes no detections, and the senior analysts are quietly carrying the queue. The hiring manager asks what went wrong in the loop. Your honest answer?

choices.label: 'A needs more time — juniors take a year.'
choices.feedback: Time doesn't fix a hiring-criteria error. The loop selected for trivia, and trivia is what you got.

choices.label: 'We hired the credential instead of the work sample. Next loop: paid work-sample exercise weighted above trivia.'
choices.feedback: The fix is structural: work samples predict job performance; trivia predicts interview performance. Change the loop.

steps.text: B is hired. Month two: B's detection rule catches a real intrusion the commercial feed missed. But B's ticket hygiene is sloppy and documentation thin. How do you develop the hire?

choices.label: Put B on a PIP for the documentation gaps
choices.feedback: A PIP for a two-month junior who just caught an intrusion is how you lose exactly the people you fought to hire.

choices.label: Pair B with a senior for ticket hygiene, make documentation part of the detection-ship checklist, and keep B writing rules
choices.feedback: Develop the weakness without punishing the strength: checklists and pairing for hygiene, full runway for detections. That's what good leads do.

simulations.debrief: Hire for demonstrated work, develop the gaps structurally. The roles library's hiring lesson: work samples predict performance, credentials predict interviews — and juniors with spikes need scaffolding, not PIPs.

consoleSims.title: Provision the Team
consoleSims.brief: New SOC analysts start Monday. Build their identities: users, groups, least-privilege policies, and MFA.

tasks.hint: Users section: add user to group form — USER soc-analyst-01, GROUP soc-tier1.
Users section: enable MFA form with USER soc-analyst-01.

consoleSims.debrief: Onboarding is identity work: named users, role-based groups, least-privilege membership, MFA from day one. The access review in sim-4 is what happens when this step is skipped.

consoleSims.title: Work the Help Desk Queue
consoleSims.brief: Tier 1 lives in the queue. Create, assign, and advance tickets by the book.

tasks.instruction: Create a P3 ticket titled 'New hire needs laptop imaged'.
tasks.hint: New ticket: TITLE exactly as given, PRIORITY P3.

tasks.instruction: Add a note to INC-9001: 'User confirmed VPN stable after reimage.'

params.text: User confirmed VPN stable after reimage.

tasks.hint: Add note form: INC-9001 with the exact text.

tasks.instruction: Resolve INC-9001 with resolution 'Reimaged; VPN stable.'
tasks.hint: Resolve form: INC-9001, resolution exactly 'Reimaged; VPN stable.'

consoleSims.debrief: Tier 1 is the profession's foundation: every ticket gets an owner, a note trail, and a real resolution. The escalation ladder in sim-3 only works if tier 1 does this part right.

consoleSims.title: Assign Cloud RBAC
consoleSims.brief: Map the new data analyst to their role: resource group, and a least-privilege RBAC assignment.

tasks.instruction: Create a resource group named 'rg-analytics' in location 'eastus'.
tasks.hint: Resource Groups: NAME rg-analytics, LOCATION eastus.

tasks.instruction: Create a virtual network in 'rg-analytics' with CIDR 10.5.0.0/16.
tasks.hint: Virtual Networks: RESOURCE GROUP rg-analytics, CIDR 10.5.0.0/16.

tasks.instruction: Assign the 'Reader' role to principal 'data-analyst-02' on scope 'rg-analytics'.
tasks.hint: Use the RBAC assignment (assign-rbac): SCOPE rg-analytics, PRINCIPAL data-analyst-02, ROLE Reader.

consoleSims.debrief: Cloud roles are the roles library made concrete: scopes, principals, and named roles instead of shared admin passwords. Reader first — elevate only with a ticket.

consoleSims.title: Set File Permissions by Role
consoleSims.brief: Translate role boundaries into file permissions: restrict the app config to its service account.

tasks.instruction: Set mode 640 on /etc/app.conf — owner and group read, nothing for others.

consoleSims.debrief: Least privilege starts at the filesystem: every file has an owning role, and permissions encode exactly what that role needs. The access review catches what this step prevents.

terminalMissions.title: Survey the Directory
terminalMissions.brief: Orient: list the workspace and read the notes.
terminalMissions.success_message: Directory surveyed. Know the org chart before the incident.

terminalMissions.title: Draft the RACI
terminalMissions.brief: Write the VPN service's RACI line to raci.txt.

checks.hint: Type: echo "vpn owner: netops-lead" > raci.txt (no output on success).

terminalMissions.success_message: RACI drafted. Unowned services are outages waiting for a date.

terminalMissions.title: Audit the Roster
terminalMissions.brief: Count RACI lines and search for the owner entry.
terminalMissions.success_message: Roster audited. Every service, an owner. Every owner, named.

terminalMissions.title: Seal the Skills Matrix
terminalMissions.brief: Hash your skills-matrix snapshot — the honest baseline, tamper-evident.

checks.hint: Type: sha256sum troubleshooting-9 architecture-4 — the real hash plus your scores are echoed.

terminalMissions.success_message: Matrix sealed. Measure honestly — the matrix is a plan, not a verdict.

terminalMissions.title: Verify the Environment
terminalMissions.success_message: Identity verified. Know your role before you play it.

terminalMissions.title: Read the Incident Log
terminalMissions.brief: The outage left a log trail. Read its edges and find the errors.

checks.hint: Type: grep ERROR logs/app.log — the timeout error appears.

terminalMissions.success_message: Log read. Post-mortems start with the timeline.

terminalMissions.title: Check Directory Reachability
terminalMissions.brief: Verify the identity provider is reachable: DNS and ping.
terminalMissions.success_message: IdP reachable. Identity is the perimeter — verify the road to it.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about the most technically difficult problem you have run into — a homelab, a broken environment, anything — and how you solved it.
points: Pick ONE problem with a real evidence trail: the symptom, what you measured, the hypothesis you tested
Show the loop: scope, observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate — interviewers score the method, not just the fix
Name the tools (VM build, networking, logs) and the lesson it taught you
Close with the result in concrete terms: what works now that did not before
pitfalls: Choosing a story with no real obstacle (“I Googled it” is not a story)
Skipping validation — saying it worked without proving it
Rambling past two minutes without reaching the result

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you dealt with a frustrated customer or user while something was broken.
points: Lead with empathy and ownership: acknowledge the impact before the technical detail
Show translation: what you told them, in their language, plus the timeline you committed to
Show judgment: the narrow fix you chose and what you refused to do (e.g., disabling the control to clear the symptom)
Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one
pitfalls: Badmouthing the customer to sound decisive
Promising a timeline you could not keep
Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened
Tie their model to your instincts: deny-by-default matches how you already think about trust
Show service orientation: the Cyber Hero culture rewards the 2 a.m. helper — give an example of being one
Name one forward-looking reason: Zero Trust, the MSP mission, or the bootcamp community investment
pitfalls: Generic flattery with no specifics about the company
Leading with compensation, title, or location convenience
Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?
points: The scattered signals and why nobody had connected them yet
The specific links you drew between them (shared host, time, infrastructure)
What the bigger picture turned out to be and what action it drove
What the experience taught you about investigating
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you connected scattered clues into a bigger picture that others had missed.

pitfalls: Claiming you fixed everything: credibility comes from trade-offs, not heroics.
Hiding the constraint: the limitation is what makes the prioritization story real.
No metric: 'better' needs a before-and-after.
points: The constraint (time, budget, staff) and the size of the backlog
How you decided what mattered most (what was reachable, what was critical)
What you did first and what you deliberately deferred
The measurable result of the prioritization
behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to prioritize risks or fixes with limited time or resources. How did you decide what came first?

pitfalls: Reciting jargon to a non-technical audience and calling it communication.
Skipping the audience's reaction: did they actually understand and act?
Making yourself the hero instead of the translator.
points: The technical finding and why it mattered
Who the audience was and what they cared about
How you reframed it (a picture, an analogy, a story)
What decision or action the audience took because they understood
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you explained a complex technical finding to a non-technical audience and it changed a decision.
Tell me about a time you used automation or AI to solve a security problem.
points: The repetitive security task and what it cost in analyst time
The automation or AI approach you built and how you validated it
Measured outcome: time saved, detection gained, false positives changed
pitfalls: Describing the tool but never the validation
No measurable outcome

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to decide whether to trust an automated security decision.
points: The stakes of the automated action and its blast radius
How you verified before acting (or the gate you built)
What happened and what you would automate differently next time
pitfalls: Saying you always trust the tool
No mention of blast radius or reversibility

sections.heading: Company facts (verified)
items: Founded 2017 in Orlando, FL — Danny Jenkins (CEO), Sami Jenkins (COO), John Carolan (QA)
Philosophy: deny-by-default / default-deny — approve known-good, deny the rest
Customers: 70,000+ organizations, sold heavily through the MSP channel
Funding: $190M Series F, July 2026 (Elephant-led); ~730 employees
Interview address: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando, FL 32810
Culture: in-office 5 days/week; free lunch; post-offer background + drug screening

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers
Ringfencing — constrains allowed apps: app-to-app, file, registry, network
Storage Control — USB/device policy by serial, user, file type, encryption
Elevation Control — just-in-time per-app admin, no standing rights
Network Control — host firewall; port/IP/dynamic-ACL rules; ZTNA foundation
Web Control — agent-based DNS/URL category filtering, works off-network
Cyber Hero MDR — 24/7/365 US-based response, ~60-second average
Testing Environment — one-button VDI sandbox; checks AV flags, canary files, registry changes

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.

checklist: Sixty-second company brief rehearsed out loud: year, city, philosophy, three products, one milestone
Two STAR stories ready: hardest technical problem; a frustrated customer or user
“Why ThreatLocker / why cybersecurity” answer tied to prevention and service, not slogans
Ringfencing explained in one plain-English sentence (the Word-on-a-leash version)
Elevation Control answer ready: just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed, ringfenced, logged
Triage loop memorized: scope → observe → hypothesize → smallest safe change → validate → explain
Three questions to ask them: team on-call shape, approval SLA expectations, what “most helpful” looks like on the team
Logistics: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando FL; in-office role; ID and references ready
Define your crown jewels before you model anything.
Build the asset-and-access graph from live sources (scans, configs, identity), not from the CMDB alone.
Model vulnerabilities AND misconfigurations as exploit edges.
Compute shortest attack paths to each crown jewel; name the choke points.
Prioritize remediation by path risk, not by raw severity score.
Express at least one access policy as a relationship path (ReBAC pilot).
Baseline approved communication edges per segment; alert on first-seen edges.
Brief the next incident or risk review with the graph, not a spreadsheet.
Can you explain supervised vs unsupervised vs anomaly detection with a security example for each?
Can you name three log features you would engineer for a C2 detector and why?
Can you walk through a UEBA alert (baseline, deviation, verification) end to end?
Can you explain the precision/recall tradeoff and how you would set a threshold for a fatigued SOC?
Can you define concept drift and describe a retraining process?
Can you distinguish direct vs indirect prompt injection and jailbreaking?
Can you explain tool poisoning in the MCP ecosystem and three controls against it?
Can you describe insecure output handling and how you would validate agent output?
Can you name the three adversarial ML attack classes and one defense for evasion?
Can you design a SOAR playbook gate: what automates freely, what needs human approval?

media.title: Allowlisting vs blocklisting: default-deny vs default-allow
media.caption: Default-deny stops unknown code without a signature; default-allow runs it until one exists.
media.alt: Side-by-side comparison: on the left, a default-deny gate runs known-good payroll software and denies unknown ransomware with no signature needed; on the right, a default-allow gate runs both until the ransomware is recognized as bad.

media.title: Ringfencing: four leashes on an allowed application
media.caption: Word stays approved, but it cannot spawn PowerShell, read the credential store, or reach the internet — while opening its document is allowed.
media.alt: An approved Word application inside a dashed containment ring: arrows show PowerShell launch denied, credential-store registry access denied, external network denied, and document file access allowed.

media.title: The Zero Trust endpoint stack
media.caption: Five deny-by-default layers — Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Elevation, Storage, Network — watched by Web Control, the Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and the Cyber Hero MDR team.
media.alt: A vertical stack of five layers from Allowlisting at the foundation up through Ringfencing, Elevation Control, Storage Control, and Network Control, with side boxes for Web Control, Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and Cyber Hero MDR.

media.title: Application-request triage flow
media.caption: Gather evidence first, then branch: trusted gets a scoped rule, unknown goes to the sandbox, malicious gets a documented deny.
media.alt: Flowchart from request arrival through evidence gathering to a decision diamond branching into three outcomes: approve with a scoped rule, detonate in the Testing Environment then ringfence, or deny with documented evidence.
Diagram of four labeled nodes (user, host, file, domain, IP) joined by labeled directed edges such as logged into, downloaded, and resolved to, illustrating graph vocabulary.
media.caption: Nodes are the things; edges are the relationships. Attackers move along the edges.
media.title: Graph vocabulary: nodes and edges

media.alt: Attack graph with four nodes in a chain: external attacker to VPN gateway to file server to customer database, with a dead-end branch to a printer, showing the shortest path to the crown jewel.
media.caption: The shortest path to the crown jewel is length 3. Break the choke point and the campaign dies.
media.title: Attack graph: shortest path to the crown jewels

media.alt: Seven kill-chain stages as connected graph nodes: reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, actions. Three alerts are annotated at delivery, installation, and command and control.
media.caption: Three 'unrelated' alerts, one kill-chain subgraph. Correlate by shared entities, not by severity.
media.title: Kill chain as a graph

media.caption: Valid credentials are not enough. The graph checks device trust, history, and relationships on every request.
media.title: Zero Trust runs on relationships
ML detection pipeline: telemetry to triage
media.caption: How raw telemetry becomes scored alerts: features feed the model, the model scores, analysts triage top-down — and analyst verdicts feed retraining.
media.alt: Flow diagram: telemetry sources feed feature extraction, which feeds an ML model, which outputs scored alerts into an analyst triage queue, with a feedback arrow for retraining.

media.title: UEBA: baseline vs deviation
media.caption: UEBA learns each user's normal hours, locations, and volumes, then scores deviations from that baseline.
